title: One Building, From Land to Legacy
summary: This week follows one hypothetical 100-unit apartment building through its whole life: land, approvals, finance, construction, lease-up, hold or refinance, and what it becomes in an estate. Today sets out the case, its master numbers and the gates it must pass. Every bench of the faculty will test it this week.
body:
A building is one decision made many times. This week we follow a single hypothetical apartment building from the land to the legacy, and the lesson is that every gate asks the same question: does the number the whole building depends on still hold?

Recall

Q. What must happen before a manager awards a contract to its own construction company?

A. Disclosure, competing bids, a capped fee, audit rights for the investor and written approval before award.

Q. What is key-person risk, and how does a growing company reduce it?

A. The danger that the business depends on one person. It is reduced by a named second person with authority, written systems, key-person insurance and clear succession terms.

Q. What does it mean to lead as owner on a construction project?

A. To hold the authority to decide, run a steady meeting cadence, escalate early and hold every party to its commitments, including being willing to terminate a contractor when the contract allows.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, for 129 weeks you have studied the parts. This week you assemble them. The case is one hypothetical building, invented for teaching, with round numbers. It is not your project and resembles no real one. The value of the exercise is that each part of the course turns out to depend on the others. A cost overrun in construction becomes a refinancing problem; a refinancing problem becomes a family problem. Seeing the whole chain once is how you learn to protect it.

The case

A mid-rise apartment building of 100 units on a serviced urban lot, built to hold. The developer, a small company with one institutional equity partner, plans to complete it, lease it, refinance it onto a long-term loan and keep it for decades. Here are the master numbers, all hypothetical.

LineHypothetical amount
Land3,000,000 dollars
Hard costs22,000,000 dollars
Soft costs4,000,000 dollars
Finance costs and interest2,000,000 dollars
Contingency1,000,000 dollars
Total cost32,000,000 dollars
Stabilised net operating income1,920,000 dollars a year

Net operating income (NOI) is the rent left after operating costs and before debt service and income tax. It comes from 100 units at an average of 2,400 dollars a month, which is 2,880,000 dollars a year of gross potential rent, less 5 percent vacancy and bad debt of 144,000 dollars, plus 64,000 dollars of parking and other income, giving 2,800,000 dollars of effective gross income. Operating costs of 880,000 dollars leave 1,920,000 dollars of NOI.

The first worked example is the one the whole building rests on. Yield on cost is stabilised NOI divided by total cost: 1,920,000 divided by 32,000,000 is 6.0 percent. If similar stabilised buildings trade at a capitalisation rate, or cap rate, of 5.0 percent, the building is worth 1,920,000 divided by 0.05, which is 38,400,000 dollars. The development spread is 6.0 less 5.0, one percentage point, and the profit on cost is 6,400,000 dollars, or 20 percent. That one percentage point is the entire reason to build. Everything this week is about protecting it.

Say that out loud now.

Six percent yield on cost against a five percent cap rate. One point of spread. Everything else protects that point.

The gates

The building passes seven gates, each a go or no-go decision with a named owner. Gate one, land: is the price supported by the residual, the value minus every other cost and the required profit? Gate two, entitlement: does the approved envelope deliver 100 units, or fewer? Gate three, finance: does a construction lender commit on terms the pro forma can carry? Gate four, design and buyout: do bought-out prices confirm the 22,000,000 dollar hard cost? Gate five, completion: is the building finished, certified for occupancy and in balance? Gate six, stabilisation: does lease-up reach the rent and occupancy the NOI assumes? Gate seven, the long hold: does the permanent loan take out the construction loan, and is the ownership structure ready for the people who will inherit it?

A second worked example shows how the gates connect. Suppose buyout at gate four comes in 1,500,000 dollars over, and contingency covers only 1,000,000 dollars. Total cost rises to 32,500,000 dollars. Yield on cost falls to 1,920,000 divided by 32,500,000, about 5.91 percent. The spread shrinks from 1.0 to about 0.91 points. Not a disaster. But the same overrun also leaves the construction loan out of balance by 500,000 dollars until equity is deposited, and it reduces the margin by which the permanent loan, on Day 3, must cover the construction loan. One number, three consequences, three gates later.

What each bench will test

The rest of the week puts the case in front of each seat at the table, and each asks its own version of the same question. Ford and Roman ask what single assumption could break it, using a real building that broke on one. Priya asks whether the loan that builds it can be repaid by the loan that holds it. LEX asks whether the documents that carry it from land to legacy actually fit together. Sage works backward from the finished value to the most the land is worth, and shows how little it takes to make that number vanish. Marco runs the meeting at which the contractor hands the building to its owner and its operator.

Listen for the pattern. Every bench is protecting the same one point of spread from a different direction. A cost overrun spends it from below; a rising cap rate spends it from above; a higher interest rate spends it at the refinance; a missing record or an unproven life-safety system spends it later, as a claim, a lawsuit or a building that cannot be insured. The faculty disagrees about methods. It does not disagree about the point.

How the best do it

The most disciplined institutional owners keep one living document for each building, often called the investment memorandum, and update it at every gate rather than writing a new story each time. Each version shows the same master table, what has changed since the last gate and why, and the decision taken. A small developer can copy this exactly: one memo, one master table, a dated change log, reviewed at each gate by the people who must approve it.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: how land, construction costs, interest and the later refinance are treated depends on local law and decides after-tax return; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: a single-purpose company owns the building so that its risks stay inside it. Banking: the construction lender and the permanent lender test different numbers, and both must be satisfied. Governance: each gate has a named owner and a written decision. Estate: a building held for decades will outlive the plan unless the shares are held in a structure designed for heirs. Exit: the planned exit is a refinance, not a sale, so the exit risk is the interest rate on the day the construction loan matures.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, tax adviser, structural engineer of record and an appraiser at the gates where each applies.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating each gate as its own project and missing that a small change in one moves the master number at every later gate. The control is the single investment memo with the master table re-run at every gate, so a change in cost, rent, rate or cap rate shows its effect on the spread immediately.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner tracks the budget and forgets the spread. A building can be on budget and still fail if the cap rate rises from 5.0 to 6.0 percent, because at that point the spread is gone.

Callback

In Week 1, Remi described the developer's lifecycle, its value levers and its go/no-go gates. This week is that first lesson with numbers in every cell. In Week 10, Sage taught NOI, cap rate, yield on cost and development spread. Here they become one sentence: six against five, one point of spread to defend.

Recap

One hypothetical 100-unit building, 32,000,000 dollars of cost, 1,920,000 dollars of NOI, a 6.0 percent yield on cost against a 5.0 percent cap rate. Seven gates, each with an owner. One memo with one master table, re-run at every gate.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: Stuyvesant Town, a building whose every gate leaned on one assumption.
checklist: I can state the case's yield on cost, cap rate and development spread from memory.
I can derive NOI from rent, vacancy, other income and operating costs.
I know the seven gates and who owns each decision.
I keep one investment memo per building with one master table.
I re-run the spread at every gate, not only the budget.
I trace any change in cost, rent, rate or cap rate through every later gate.
I know which professional must sign off at each gate.
head: Field checklist
speak: This week follows one hypothetical 100-unit apartment building from land to legacy. Total cost is 32,000,000 dollars: land 3,000,000, hard costs 22,000,000, soft costs 4,000,000, finance costs 2,000,000 and contingency 1,000,000. At an average rent of 2,400 dollars a month, less 5 percent vacancy, plus other income and less operating costs, net operating income is 1,920,000 dollars. That is a 6.0 percent yield on cost. Similar buildings trade at a 5.0 percent cap rate, so the building is worth 38,400,000 dollars, a 20 percent profit on cost. The one point of spread between six and five is the entire reason to build. The building passes seven gates: land, entitlement, finance, design and buyout, completion, stabilisation and the long hold. A change at any gate moves the spread at every later gate. So I keep one investment memo with one master table, and I re-run the spread every time.
terms: Yield on cost — stabilised net operating income divided by total development cost.
Development spread — yield on cost minus the market cap rate, the margin that justifies building rather than buying.
Investment memorandum — the single written case for a project, updated at each gate with a dated record of changes and decisions.

hostile.q: Your whole case rests on a 5.0 percent cap rate. What happens if it is 5.5 percent when you finish?
hostile.a: The building is worth about 34,900,000 dollars instead of 38,400,000, and the profit on cost falls from about 20 percent to about 9 percent. It is still worth more than it cost, which is why I hold a long-term loan rather than selling. I carry that case in the memo, and the permanent loan is sized on income and debt service coverage, not on the cap rate, so the refinance survives it. If the cap rate moved before land closing, I would reprice the land.

role: Failure forensics, with Roman on risk and the lender's view
title: Stuyvesant Town 2006 to 2010: Every Gate Leaned on One Assumption
summary: Stuyvesant Town and Peter Cooper Village were bought in 2006 on a plan that depended on converting rent-regulated apartments to market rents. The plan moved too slowly, a court ruling went against it, and in 2010 the owners handed the property to creditors. Seven steps show how one assumption passed through every gate unchallenged, producing Rule 130.
body:
The Stuyvesant Town purchase did not fail at one gate. It passed every gate leaning on the same assumption, and when that assumption failed, there was no gate left that had tested it independently.

Recall

Q. In the waterfall Sage worked, in what order is cash paid?

A. Capital back first, then the compounded preferred return, then the split between investors and the sponsor's promote.

Q. Why does a growing company need written systems rather than a founder's memory?

A. So that decisions, approvals and knowledge survive the absence of any one person, and so lenders and investors can see how the company actually works.

Q. What is an owner's escalation path?

A. The agreed route by which an unresolved issue moves from the site team to senior people on each side within set times, so problems reach a decision-maker before they reach a dispute.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this week's case is a building held for income from land to legacy. Stuyvesant Town is the most studied failure of exactly that kind of asset: apartments bought to hold, financed on a plan for rising income. Roman sits with me because the root cause is the lender's view of income. The case appeared earlier in the course from other angles; today we read it as a lifecycle.

Step 1: the timeline

Stuyvesant Town and Peter Cooper Village are two adjoining apartment complexes in Manhattan with about 11,000 apartments, built after the Second World War by the insurer Metropolitan Life. In late 2006 MetLife sold them at auction to a venture led by Tishman Speyer and BlackRock, at a price widely reported as a record for a single residential property in the United States. Many of the apartments were rent-stabilised, which limited how much rents could rise. In October 2009 New York's highest court, in a case brought by tenants and known as Roberts, ruled that apartments had been improperly removed from rent regulation while the property received a particular tax benefit. In January 2010 the owners defaulted and turned the property over to their creditors. It was later sold to new owners.

Step 2: the key decisions

The purchase price was set by a competitive auction. The buyers financed it with a large senior loan and several layers of mezzanine debt, and set aside reserves intended to cover the shortfall between the income the buildings produced and the debt service, while the business plan raised income. The plan was to move apartments from regulated to market rents as tenants left and to improve the property.

Step 3: the assumptions

One assumption carried everything: that regulated apartments would convert to market rents fast enough, and in large enough numbers, to raise income above debt service before the reserves ran out. A second assumption, less visible, was that the legal route to deregulation would hold.

Step 4: the incentives

An auction rewards the bidder who believes most strongly in the business plan. Lenders at the time were lending against projected income, not current income. Fees and the size of the deal rewarded getting it done. No party at the table was paid to say that today's income did not support the price.

Say that out loud now.

When every gate leans on the same assumption, the gates are not independent. They are one gate, passed several times.

Step 5: the warning signs ignored

Roman's view: the income at purchase did not cover the debt service on its own. That is the warning sign in one line. A worked example of the shape, with hypothetical round numbers. A building earns 50,000,000 dollars a year of NOI. Debt service is 80,000,000 dollars. A reserve of 120,000,000 dollars covers the gap of 30,000,000 dollars a year for four years. If the plan raises NOI by 10,000,000 dollars a year, the gap closes in year four, just as the reserve runs out. If NOI rises by only 5,000,000 dollars a year, the reserve is gone in about three and a half years with the gap still open. The thinner the reserve against the plan's pace, the less any delay can be absorbed. Tenant turnover in rent-regulated housing is slow by nature, and the legal challenge to deregulation was a known risk while it was being litigated.

Step 6: the point of no return

The point of no return was the purchase itself, at a price that only the business plan could repay. After closing, every later event, the slow turnover, the falling market of 2008 and the 2009 ruling, worked against a structure with no margin. A second hypothetical example: had the price been set so that current income covered debt service at 1.0 times, the business plan would have been upside. Set so that it covered only about 0.6 times, the plan became the whole of the repayment.

Step 7: the root cause

The root cause was underwriting a held building on income that the law, the tenants and the market had not yet allowed, and letting that single assumption pass through the price, the debt and the reserves without an independent test at any gate.

What an independent test would have looked like

Reverse engineer the case and ask what test at each gate would have changed the outcome. At the price: a valuation on current income alone, with the business plan shown separately as upside. At the debt: a loan sized to cover debt service from current income, with any further borrowing released only as the plan was actually delivered, apartment by apartment. At the reserves: a break-even showing how slowly income could rise before the reserve ran out, compared honestly with the historic turnover rate. At the legal route: a written opinion on the deregulation risk while it was being litigated, priced as a scenario rather than dismissed. None of these tests is unusual. Each would have been run by a different person with a different incentive, which is exactly what made it independent.

Roman's summary: a lender who funds the plan before it is delivered has become an equity investor without being paid like one.

The lifecycle lesson for our case

Apply this to the 100-unit building. Its master number is 1,920,000 dollars of NOI at 2,400 dollars a month. Each gate must test that rent independently. At land: is 2,400 dollars supported by comparable buildings today, or by a forecast? At finance: does the lender size the loan on that rent or on a lower one? At lease-up: does the absorption pace support it? If each gate simply repeats the original rent, the building has one test, not seven.

The prevention rule

Rule 130: At every gate, re-test the one assumption the whole building depends on against evidence available today, and never let a price, a loan or a reserve depend on income the law, the tenants or the market have not yet allowed.

This is a summary of widely reported events for teaching; read the primary accounts and the court decision before citing them in a meeting.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is the comfort of consistency: the same rent appearing at every gate looks like confirmation when it is only repetition. The control is an independent source for the master assumption at each gate: comparables at land, the lender's own rent at finance, signed leases at lease-up.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads this case as being about rent regulation. It is about any income that has to be created after you have paid for it. A hotel conversion, a lease-up in a new submarket and a rent increase after renovation all carry the same risk.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman taught stress tests: break-evens, downside and severe cases, and triggers. A break-even test at purchase, how slowly can income rise before the reserve is exhausted, would have shown the margin in one number. Run that test at every gate of our case.

Recap

Stuyvesant Town was priced, financed and reserved on one assumption about rising income. Turnover was slow, a court ruling cut the route, and the owners handed the property to creditors in 2010. Rule 130: re-test the master assumption at every gate against today's evidence.

Next: Priya on The Money: the capital stack of our case from construction loan to permanent loan.
checklist: I can name the one assumption my building depends on.
I re-test that assumption at every gate against evidence available today.
I use a different source for it at each gate: comparables, the lender's view, signed leases.
Current income covers debt service before any business plan is counted.
I know how long my reserve lasts if the plan moves at half speed.
I treat income that must be created after purchase as upside, not repayment.
I read primary accounts before citing a failure case.
head: Field checklist
speak: Stuyvesant Town and Peter Cooper Village, about 11,000 apartments in Manhattan, were sold by MetLife in late 2006 to a venture led by Tishman Speyer and BlackRock at a reported record price. The plan depended on converting rent-stabilised apartments to market rents as tenants left, with reserves covering the gap between income and debt service in the meantime. Turnover was slow, the market fell in 2008, and in October 2009 New York's highest court ruled in the Roberts case that apartments had been improperly deregulated. In January 2010 the owners defaulted and handed the property to creditors. The root cause was one assumption, income not yet allowed, passing through the price, the debt and the reserves without an independent test. Rule 130: at every gate, re-test the one assumption the whole building depends on against evidence available today, and never let a price, loan or reserve depend on income not yet allowed.
terms: Rent stabilisation — a form of rent regulation that limits rent increases on covered apartments.
Reserve — cash set aside at closing to cover a known shortfall, such as debt service before income rises.
Master assumption — the single input on which a project's viability depends most.

hostile.q: Your pro forma uses 2,400 dollars a month at every stage. Where did that number come from, and who has tested it?
hostile.a: It came from comparable buildings leased in the last twelve months, adjusted for unit size, and I will show you the list. At finance, I want your appraiser's independent rent, and I will size my plan to the lower of the two. At lease-up, signed leases replace both. If any of those sources comes in below 2,400 dollars, I re-run the spread before the next gate rather than carrying the old number forward.

rule: Rule 130: At every gate, re-test the one assumption the whole building depends on against evidence available today, and never let a price, a loan or a reserve depend on income the law, the tenants or the market have not yet allowed.

title: The Case's Capital Stack: From Construction Loan to Permanent Loan
summary: Follow the case's money: the construction loan sized on cost, the equity that goes in first, and the permanent loan sized on income that must repay the construction loan. A rate rise shows how the take-out can fall short. Warrick's Wealth Ledger and a monthly thread on decision journals close the lesson.
body:
A building held for income is financed twice: once on what it costs, and once on what it earns. The first loan is sized on the budget; the second on the rent. The gap between them is where held buildings are won or lost.

Recall

Q. In an institutional committee, what should you do immediately after stating your fees?

A. Stop talking and let them read the waterfall. Silence after a number is credible.

Q. What is the difference between a company's growth plan and its funding plan?

A. The growth plan says what the company will build; the funding plan says where every dollar comes from and when it must be repaid. Growth without a matched funding plan is a duration mismatch.

Q. When should an owner consider terminating a contractor?

A. Only on grounds and through the steps the contract allows, after notices and cure periods, with records in place, legal advice taken and a replacement plan ready.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a long-term owner's wealth is made at the moment the construction loan is replaced by a permanent loan. If the permanent loan is large enough, you keep the building on patient money. If it is not, you must find equity at the worst possible time, or sell. Today we run the case's money from start to finish.

The construction stack

In plain English: during construction the lender lends a share of the cost, and you put in the rest first.

The professional framing: the construction lender sizes the loan on loan to cost (LTC), the loan divided by total cost. Suppose the lender offers 65 percent LTC, a commercial term, not a standard. The first worked example: 65 percent of 32,000,000 dollars is 20,800,000 dollars of loan. Equity is the other 11,200,000 dollars. As is common practice, equity goes in first, so the lender's money is at risk only after yours. The developer's company contributes part of the equity and the institutional partner the rest, under a joint venture agreement. The interest reserve inside the 2,000,000 dollar finance budget pays interest during construction and lease-up, because the building earns nothing until it has tenants.

The permanent loan

In plain English: once the building is leased, a long-term lender lends against the rent, not the cost.

The professional framing: the permanent lender tests several limits and lends the smallest. The debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) is NOI divided by annual debt service. Suppose the lender requires 1.25 times, at a 6 percent interest rate on a 30-year amortising loan. Maximum annual debt service is 1,920,000 dollars divided by 1.25, which is 1,536,000 dollars. At 6 percent over 30 years, the annual payment is about 7.19 cents per dollar borrowed, so the loan is about 1,536,000 divided by 0.0719, about 21,350,000 dollars. Check the other limits. Loan to value is 21,350,000 over 38,400,000, about 56 percent, well under a typical 65 percent limit. Debt yield, NOI over the loan, is about 9.0 percent. Here the coverage ratio binds.

The permanent loan of about 21,350,000 dollars repays the construction loan of 20,800,000 dollars with about 550,000 dollars to spare, before refinancing costs. Call it a modest cash-out of a few hundred thousand dollars once fees are paid. The building is now on a 30-year loan with annual debt service of 1,536,000 dollars, leaving about 384,000 dollars a year of cash flow before tax and capital reserves.

Say that out loud now.

The construction loan is sized on cost. The permanent loan is sized on income. The take-out works only if the income loan is at least as big as the cost loan.

The second worked example: the rate rises

Now suppose that during construction the permanent rate rises from 6 to 7 percent. The annual payment per dollar rises to about 7.98 cents. The maximum loan becomes 1,536,000 divided by 0.0798, about 19,240,000 dollars. The construction loan is still 20,800,000 dollars. The take-out falls short by about 1,560,000 dollars. Nothing went wrong on site. The rent is the same, the building is full, and you must still find 1,560,000 dollars of new equity or a second loan to close, or extend the construction loan and wait.

The controls are known in advance. Size the construction loan with the permanent loan in mind, test the take-out at a higher rate before you commit, hedge the rate if the cost is reasonable, and hold liquidity or committed partner equity to cover a shortfall. Rule 129 applies directly: the term of the money must match the asset, and the take-out is where the short money becomes long.

What is left after the loan

The 384,000 dollars of cash flow after debt service is not yet spendable. A held building needs a capital reserve for things that wear out: roofs, boilers, elevators, unit interiors. Suppose, as a hypothetical commercial practice, the owner sets aside 300 dollars per unit per year, 30,000 dollars for 100 units. Cash flow falls to about 354,000 dollars. On 11,200,000 dollars of equity, that is a cash-on-cash return of about 3.2 percent, before income tax.

That figure surprises beginners. A building with a 20 percent development profit pays its owners barely 3 percent a year in cash at first. The rest of the return is in the value created and in the income growing over time while the loan amortises. That is the long-term owner's model from Week 129: little cash early, compounding equity later. If an owner needs cash now, this is the wrong model for that money, and the right answer is to say so before building rather than to borrow more against the building later.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet, this building appears as your share of its equity value: value less the permanent loan, multiplied by your ownership. At a 5.0 percent cap rate, 38,400,000 less 21,350,000 is about 17,050,000 dollars of equity value for all owners, against 11,200,000 dollars invested. Your share is real but illiquid; you cannot spend it without selling or borrowing more. So the ledger entry carries two columns: equity value, and cash available within twelve months. A strong first column and an empty second column is how wealthy developers become forced sellers. A licensed adviser is required before you act.

Decision journals, a monthly thread

Before you commit to the construction loan, write one page in your decision journal: the permanent rate you assumed, the take-out you expect, the shortfall at a rate one point higher and what you will do if it happens. Date it and seal it.

When the refinance closes, open the page and compare. The point is not to grade yourself on the rate, which nobody controls. It is to learn whether you prepared for the case you could see, and to make the next page better.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a construction loan larger than the permanent loan that must repay it. The control is a take-out test at commitment, at the expected rate and at a rate at least one point higher, with the shortfall funded or covered by committed equity before construction starts.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner asks the construction lender for the largest loan available. A smaller construction loan, sized to fit inside a stressed permanent loan, is often the cheaper loan once the refinance is counted.

Callback

In Week 36, Priya taught sizing to the binding limit: DSCR, debt yield, loan to value and loan to cost, and taking the smallest. Today that idea appears twice in one building, once for each loan, and the gap between the two answers is the refinance risk.

Recap

The case borrows 20,800,000 dollars at 65 percent of cost, with 11,200,000 dollars of equity first. At 6 percent and 1.25 times coverage, the permanent loan of about 21,350,000 dollars repays it. At 7 percent, it falls about 1,560,000 dollars short. Test the take-out at a higher rate before committing.

Next: LEX on The Rules: the chain of documents that carries the building from land to legacy.
checklist: I size the construction loan with the permanent loan in mind.
I test the take-out at the expected rate and at least one point higher.
I know which limit binds the permanent loan: coverage, debt yield or loan to value.
Any take-out shortfall is funded or covered by committed equity before construction.
I record equity value and twelve-month liquidity as separate ledger columns.
I write a sealed decision-journal page before committing to a construction loan.
I state that LTC, DSCR and LTV limits are commercial practice.
head: Field checklist
speak: Our hypothetical building is financed twice. During construction, the lender sizes the loan on cost: 65 percent of 32,000,000 dollars is 20,800,000, and the 11,200,000 dollars of equity goes in first. Once the building is leased, the permanent lender sizes the loan on income. With 1,920,000 dollars of net operating income and a required coverage of 1.25 times, maximum debt service is 1,536,000 dollars a year. At 6 percent over 30 years, that supports about 21,350,000 dollars, which repays the construction loan with a little to spare. But if the rate rises to 7 percent, the same income supports only about 19,240,000 dollars, and the take-out falls about 1,560,000 dollars short, with nothing wrong on site. So I test the take-out at a higher rate before committing, size the construction loan to fit, and hold committed equity for any gap. Equity value is not liquidity.
terms: Loan to cost (LTC) — the loan amount divided by total project cost, used to size construction loans.
Take-out — the permanent loan or sale that repays the construction loan.
Debt yield — net operating income divided by the loan amount, a test that ignores interest rate and amortisation.

hostile.q: If permanent rates are a point higher when you finish, how do you repay my construction loan?
hostile.a: At a point higher, the permanent loan is about 1,560,000 dollars short of your loan. That gap is covered before you fund the first draw: my partner has committed additional equity up to 2,000,000 dollars in the joint venture agreement, and I hold liquidity beside it. I have also asked for a 12-month extension option on defined tests, so we are not forced to refinance into a peak. I can show you the take-out test at both rates.

title: The Chain of Documents From Land to Legacy
summary: The case's building passes through a chain of legal documents: purchase agreement, title, approvals, loans, construction contract, occupancy, leases, and finally the structure heirs will inherit. Each document hands risk to the next. Learn the chain and the link that breaks most often.
body:
A building is carried through its life by a chain of documents, and each one hands risk to the next. Most legal failures in development are not a bad clause in one document. They are two documents that do not fit where they meet.

Recall

Q. In the Red Pen term sheet, what was wrong with "Promote: 20 percent of profits"?

A. It did not say profits after what. The promote should be a share of distributions above capital and the preferred return.

Q. What does a company's minute book prove?

A. That decisions were authorised by the right body at the right time, which lenders and buyers rely on when they ask who may bind the company.

Q. What must an owner check before relying on a contract's termination clause?

A. The grounds it allows, the notices it requires, the cure periods, the consequences for payment and what the contract says about completing the work with others.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a developer signs dozens of documents over a building's life. You do not need to draft them. You need to see how they connect, because the gaps between them are where your risk sits. This lesson walks the case's chain once, link by link. Everything here is concept; the law in each place decides how each document works. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Links one to three: land, title and approvals

The chain starts with the purchase agreement. For the case, the buyer signs a conditional purchase agreement: the 3,000,000 dollar purchase closes only if conditions are satisfied by set dates, such as satisfactory title, environmental and geotechnical reports, and zoning approval for 100 units. A condition precedent is an event that must happen before an obligation becomes binding.

A first worked example, hypothetical. The agreement gives the buyer 90 days to satisfy the zoning condition, with no right to extend. The planning authority schedules its decision for day 100. On day 91 the condition fails and, depending on the wording, the seller may be free to terminate or to renegotiate the price upward. The fix belongs in the draft: an extension right tied to the authority's timetable, a defined meaning of satisfactory approval, including the number of units, and a clear statement of what happens to the deposit.

Title comes next: the search confirms the seller owns the land and shows the easements, covenants and charges registered against it. Then the approvals: the zoning approval and any development agreement set conditions that bind the land, such as a road widening or a contribution to infrastructure. Those conditions must be priced into the 4,000,000 dollar soft-cost budget before land closes.

Links four and five: the loans and the construction contract

The construction loan agreement, the joint venture agreement and the construction contract are signed close together and must agree. The loan's conditions precedent to the first draw often require the construction contract to be signed, bonded or guaranteed, and assigned to the lender as security. The joint venture agreement says who may approve a change order and up to what value. The construction contract says how changes are priced and when notices are due.

Say that out loud now.

Every document hands risk to the next. My job is to read where they meet.

A second worked example, hypothetical. The construction contract lets the owner's project manager approve changes up to 250,000 dollars. The joint venture agreement requires the partner's approval for any change above 100,000 dollars. The loan agreement requires lender consent for changes above 200,000 dollars or 1 percent of hard cost cumulatively. A 180,000 dollar change approved by your project manager is valid under the construction contract, a breach of the joint venture agreement and inside the loan limit, but it may push cumulative changes past the lender's limit. One signature, three documents, two problems. The control is one approvals matrix, reconciled across all three documents before construction starts, that tells each person exactly what they may sign.

Links six and seven: occupancy and leases

At completion, the authority issues the certificate that allows people to occupy the building; names and procedures differ by jurisdiction. Until it is issued, no lease can begin, and the permanent lender will usually not fund. Then the leases: each one is a contract governed by landlord-tenant law, which in many places overrides what the lease says on deposits, rent increases, repairs and eviction. The rent roll the permanent lender relies on is only as good as the leases behind it, and an unenforceable rent increase is a rent the lender will not count.

A lease clause meets the law

A third worked example, hypothetical. The case's standard lease says rent rises 5 percent a year. In the jurisdiction where the building sits, suppose a statute limits annual increases on some units, or requires a set notice period before any increase. The statute overrides the lease. The pro forma that assumed 5 percent growth on every unit now overstates income, and the permanent lender, whose counsel will read both, will underwrite to the lower figure. The fix is to have the lease reviewed against landlord-tenant law before leasing begins, and to build the pro forma's rent growth from what the law allows, not from what the lease says.

The same habit applies to deposits, which many jurisdictions require to be held in a particular way, and to repairs and entry rights, where the statute often sets minimum terms. A rent roll is a legal document as much as a financial one. Professional sign-off required: a landlord-tenant lawyer in the building's jurisdiction, on the lease form and the rent-growth assumption.

The document map, in practice

Keep the map to one page per building: each document down the left, then columns for the parties, the key dates, the approval limits, the security it creates and the other documents it refers to. Update it at every gate. When a lawyer sends a draft, check it against the map before you read the rest.

The last link: the holding structure

The building is owned by a single-purpose company. The shares of that company are owned by the developer's holding company and the partner. What happens to those shares on the developer's death or incapacity is decided by the joint venture agreement, the holding company's articles and shareholder agreement, and the developer's will and powers of attorney. If the joint venture agreement gives the partner a right to buy the developer's interest on death at a formula price, the will cannot override it. Tessa's point from Week 92 applies: the estate plan must be written knowing what the business documents already say.

Professional sign-off required: real estate lawyer on the purchase and title; finance lawyer on the loans; construction lawyer on the contract; estate lawyer on the holding structure; each in the jurisdiction where the property sits.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that each document is negotiated well by a different lawyer and none of them reads the others. The control is a single document map kept by you: each document, its parties, its approval limits, its key dates and its links to the others, reviewed before each signing.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner assumes a lawyer who negotiated one document has checked it against the rest. Unless the engagement letter says so, they have not. Instruct them to.

Callback

In Week 25, LEX and Vera taught that an engagement letter defines what a professional is responsible for. Here that idea decides whether anyone checks the links. Put the cross-document review into the engagement letter of one lead counsel, by name.

Recap

The chain runs from purchase agreement to title, approvals, loans, construction contract, occupancy, leases and the holding structure. Risk passes along it, and failures happen where documents meet. Keep one approvals matrix and one document map, and instruct one lawyer to check the links.

Next: Sage on The Numbers: reverse engineering the case from its finished value back to the land price.
checklist: Every condition precedent has a date, an extension right and a defined outcome.
Approval conditions are priced into the soft-cost budget before land closes.
I keep one approvals matrix reconciled across the loan, joint venture and construction contract.
I know what the lender needs before the first draw and before the permanent loan.
I know which landlord-tenant rules override my leases.
My estate plan is written knowing what my joint venture agreement says on death.
One lead counsel is instructed in writing to check the links between documents.
head: Field checklist
speak: A building is carried through its life by a chain of documents: the purchase agreement with its conditions, the title, the approvals, the loans, the joint venture agreement, the construction contract, the occupancy certificate, the leases and the holding structure. Each hands risk to the next, and failures happen where two documents do not fit. A zoning condition that expires before the authority decides. A change order approved under the construction contract that breaches the joint venture agreement and the loan. A rent increase the lease allows and landlord-tenant law forbids. A will that cannot override a partner's right to buy on death. So I keep one approvals matrix reconciled across every document, one map of documents, dates and links, and I instruct one lead counsel in writing to check where they meet. I do not draft them. I read the joints.
terms: Condition precedent — an event that must happen before an obligation in a contract becomes binding.
Approvals matrix — a single table showing who may approve what, up to what value, under every governing document.
Rent roll — the list of a building's leases, rents, terms and deposits, relied on by lenders and buyers.

hostile.q: Your project manager approved a change your partner never saw. Is the joint venture in breach?
hostile.a: Possibly, and I will not argue it is fine. The construction contract allowed it, but the joint venture agreement required your approval above 100,000 dollars. I will send you the change, the reason and the price today and ask for ratification. I am also replacing the separate limits with one approvals matrix reconciled across the contract, the joint venture agreement and the loan, so every signature is valid under all three.

title: Reverse Engineering the Case: From Finished Value Back to Land
summary: A worked calculation that starts from the finished building's value and the return the investor requires, and works backward to the most the developer can pay for land. Then the same method shows how a half-point move in the cap rate wipes out the land value, and how much rent it takes to justify a higher price.
body:
The most important number in development is the one you calculate backward: the most you can pay for land and still earn the return. Start from the finished building and work back, and the land price stops being a negotiation and becomes arithmetic.

Recall

Q. What is the case's yield on cost, and why does it matter?

A. 6.0 percent: 1,920,000 dollars of NOI on 32,000,000 dollars of cost. Against a 5.0 percent cap rate it gives one point of development spread, the reason to build.

Q. What is a decision journal for?

A. To record a decision, its reasons and its expected outcome before the result is known, so it can be compared later and judgment can improve.

Q. What should an owner do in the first meeting after a project goes off track?

A. State the facts plainly, give the problem one owner and a date, set the next meeting and write the note the same day.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, land is the one cost you can still negotiate before anything is committed, and the one most often overpaid. A landowner names a price. A beginner checks whether the deal works at that price. A professional calculates the price at which the deal works and compares the two. This is an even week, so we reverse engineer: start from the finished outcome and work backward. All numbers are hypothetical, and the required return is commercial practice, not a standard.

Step 1: start from the finished value

The finished building earns 1,920,000 dollars of stabilised NOI. At a market cap rate of 5.0 percent, it is worth 1,920,000 divided by 0.05, which is 38,400,000 dollars.

Step 2: take out the required profit

The investor requires a profit on cost of 20 percent. If value is 120 percent of cost, then cost may be at most value divided by 1.20. That is 38,400,000 divided by 1.20, which is 32,000,000 dollars. This is the maximum total cost, everything included.

Step 3: subtract every cost except land

Hard costs 22,000,000 dollars, soft costs 4,000,000 dollars, finance costs 2,000,000 dollars and contingency 1,000,000 dollars total 29,000,000 dollars. Maximum total cost of 32,000,000 less 29,000,000 leaves 3,000,000 dollars for land. That is 30,000 dollars per unit. This is the residual land value: what is left for the land after value, profit and every other cost.

Say that out loud now.

Value, less required profit, less every other cost, equals the most I can pay for land.

Step 4: check the result two ways

First check: yield on cost. At 32,000,000 dollars of cost, 1,920,000 divided by 32,000,000 is 6.0 percent, which matches Day 1. Second check: development spread. 6.0 less 5.0 is one point, which is roughly what a developer needs to justify the risk of building over buying an existing building. The two checks agree, so the residual is consistent.

Worked example two: the cap rate moves half a point

Run the same steps at a 5.5 percent cap rate. Value is 1,920,000 divided by 0.055, about 34,909,000 dollars. Maximum cost at a 20 percent profit is 34,909,000 divided by 1.20, about 29,091,000 dollars. Subtract the 29,000,000 dollars of other costs, and about 91,000 dollars is left for land. A half-point move in the cap rate cut the supportable land price from 3,000,000 dollars to almost nothing, a fall of about 97 percent.

This is why land is the most leveraged number in the pro forma. The land is a residual: every change in value lands on it in full. A 9 percent fall in value, from 38,400,000 to about 34,909,000 dollars, removed about 97 percent of the land value. If you pay 3,000,000 dollars for land on a 5.0 percent assumption and the market moves to 5.5 percent before you build, your profit falls from 20 percent to about 9 percent. If you pay it and then also suffer a cost overrun, the profit is gone.

Worked example three: the rent that justifies a higher price

The landowner asks 4,000,000 dollars. Work backward to the rent that would justify it, holding the cap rate at 5.0 percent and the other costs fixed. Total cost becomes 33,000,000 dollars. At 20 percent profit, value must be 33,000,000 times 1.20, which is 39,600,000 dollars. NOI must be 39,600,000 times 0.05, which is 1,980,000 dollars, 60,000 dollars more than the plan. If operating costs are fixed, effective income must rise by 60,000 dollars. Gross potential rent must rise by 60,000 divided by 0.95, about 63,200 dollars, to allow for vacancy. Across 100 units and 12 months, that is about 53 dollars per unit per month: an average rent of about 2,453 dollars instead of 2,400 dollars. Strictly, a higher land price also raises finance costs slightly, so the true required rent is a little higher still.

Now the question is evidence, not hope. Are comparable buildings leasing at 2,453 dollars? If yes, 4,000,000 dollars may be supportable. If the comparables say 2,400 dollars, then paying 4,000,000 dollars means paying the landowner for rent you have not proved, which is Rule 130 in a single line.

Worked example four: a stressed cost

Now hold the cap rate at 5.0 percent and stress the hard cost instead. Suppose buyout comes in 5 percent over, 1,100,000 dollars on 22,000,000 dollars, and contingency is already committed elsewhere. Other costs rise from 29,000,000 to 30,100,000 dollars. Maximum total cost is still 32,000,000 dollars, so land can now be at most 1,900,000 dollars. A 5 percent hard-cost overrun removed about 37 percent of the supportable land value.

Put the two stresses together, a half-point cap rate rise and a 5 percent hard-cost overrun, and the residual is negative: about 29,091,000 dollars of maximum cost against 30,100,000 dollars of other costs, about 1,009,000 dollars below zero. At those numbers, the land is worth nothing to a developer who requires 20 percent, and the project should not be built at any land price. That is a valid answer, and the reverse calculation is the only method that gives it to you before you have paid for the land.

The lesson for negotiation is plain. Your offer should sit below the residual at your conservative case, not at your base case, so that one adverse move does not consume the whole profit.

Reading the reverse-engineered answer

Three outputs belong in the investment memo before any offer: the residual land value at the base cap rate, the residual at a cap rate half a point higher, and the rent required to justify the asking price. Together they tell you your walk-away price, how fragile it is, and what you would need to believe to pay more.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is calculating the residual once, at the most optimistic cap rate, and treating it as fact. The control is to calculate it at two or three cap rates and at a stressed cost, and to offer below the residual at the conservative case.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner forgets that finance costs and contingency rise with the land price and with delay, and calculates the residual as if they were fixed. Recompute them for each scenario, or at least note that the residual is slightly overstated.

Callback

In Week 31, Pax and Cole taught highest and best use and residual land value as part of desk diligence. Today is the same calculation with the whole case behind it. In Week 17, Sage taught reverse engineering a deal from public information. Here it is reverse engineering your own deal before the landowner does it for you.

Recap

Value of 38,400,000 dollars, divided by 1.20 for profit, gives a maximum cost of 32,000,000 dollars; less 29,000,000 dollars of other costs leaves 3,000,000 dollars for land. At 5.5 percent the residual is about 91,000 dollars. To justify 4,000,000 dollars, rent must be about 2,453 dollars a month.

Next: Marco on The Room: the turnover meeting at substantial completion, from contractor to owner to operator.
checklist: I calculate the residual land value before I respond to any asking price.
I run the residual at the base cap rate and at half a point higher.
I calculate the rent needed to justify the asking price.
I check the residual against yield on cost and development spread.
I recompute finance costs and contingency when land price or timing changes.
I offer below the residual at the conservative case.
I record all three outputs in the investment memo before an offer.
head: Field checklist
speak: To find the most I can pay for land, I work backward from the finished building. Net operating income of 1,920,000 dollars at a 5.0 percent cap rate gives a value of 38,400,000 dollars. The investor needs a 20 percent profit on cost, so maximum cost is value divided by 1.20: 32,000,000 dollars. Subtract 29,000,000 dollars of hard, soft, finance and contingency costs, and 3,000,000 dollars is left for land, 30,000 dollars a unit. But at a 5.5 percent cap rate, the same steps leave about 91,000 dollars. Land is a residual, so every change in value falls on it in full. If the landowner asks 4,000,000, I work back to the rent needed: about 2,453 dollars a month instead of 2,400. Then the question is evidence. If comparables do not show that rent, paying 4,000,000 means paying for income I have not proved. I offer below the residual at the conservative case.
terms: Residual land value — finished value less required profit and every non-land cost, the most a developer can pay for land.
Profit on cost — development profit divided by total cost, a common developer return measure.
Walk-away price — the highest price at which a buyer will still proceed, set before negotiation begins.

hostile.q: The landowner has another buyer at 4,000,000 dollars. Why will you not match it?
hostile.a: Because at our cost and today's rents, the land supports 3,000,000 dollars at a 5.0 percent cap rate and almost nothing at 5.5 percent. To pay 4,000,000, I need comparable rents of about 2,453 dollars a month, and the evidence today says 2,400. If the other buyer can prove that rent, they should buy it. I will offer 2,800,000 with conditions, and I will raise it only if the evidence on rent improves.

title: The Turnover Meeting: Contractor, Owner and Operator
summary: A realistic scene at substantial completion of the case's building, with the contractor, the lender's monitor, the commissioning authority and the incoming property manager at the table. Learn the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind each question and when to stay silent.
body:
Substantial completion is the moment a construction project becomes a business. The turnover meeting decides whether the building enters its long life with complete records, working systems and a clear list of what is still owed, or with arguments that last for years.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 130?

A. At every gate, re-test the one assumption the whole building depends on against evidence available today, and never let a price, a loan or a reserve depend on income not yet allowed.

Q. In a company-building meeting, what is the question behind an investor's question about your hiring plan?

A. Whether the company can deliver without depending on the founder for every decision.

Q. When an owner chairs a difficult project meeting, what should end it?

A. A read-back of every action, owner and date, and a written note circulated within a day.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, our hypothetical 100-unit building is finished. The permanent lender will not fund until occupancy is approved and leases are in place. The contractor wants its retainage released. The property manager wants to start leasing. Everyone in the room has a reason to call the building done. Your job is to decide what done means, in writing.

At the table: the general contractor's project manager, the lender's monitor, the commissioning authority, an independent engineer who verified that the building's systems work as designed, and the incoming property manager. You chair.

Scene one: the contractor's request

The contractor opens: "We are substantially complete. We would like the certificate signed today and half the retainage released this month."

The question behind the question: will the owner give up leverage before the list is closed?

Say: "Thank you. Let us agree what substantial completion means under the contract before anyone signs. I want three things: the occupancy approval in hand, the commissioning authority's report on the life-safety and building systems, and an agreed punch list with dates and values. When we have those, I will sign, and retainage moves as the contract says."

Never say: "Let's sign now and sort out the details." The details are the leverage, and once the certificate is signed, warranties and many deadlines start running.

Then stop and let the contractor answer.

Scene two: the punch list and the money

The contractor's list has 300 items. The monitor's walk found 340. A worked number to have ready, hypothetical. Suppose the open items are priced at 200,000 dollars to complete. A common practice is to hold back a multiple of that value, often one and a half to two times, from any retainage release. These multiples are commercial practice, set by the contract or negotiated, not standards. At 1.5 times, hold back 300,000 dollars. If retainage is 10 percent of a 22,000,000 dollar contract, 2,200,000 dollars, then releasing half would be 1,100,000 dollars, and the holdback leaves 800,000 dollars releasable now, subject to the contract and any statutory holdback rules. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Say: "We will merge the two lists today, price every open item, and hold back one and a half times their value from any release. The rest moves when the contract allows."

Say that out loud now.

Scene three: the commissioning authority

The commissioning authority says, carefully: "The integrated fire alarm and smoke control test passed on the second attempt. The emergency generator transfer test is scheduled for next Tuesday."

The question behind the question: will the owner occupy before the life-safety systems are proven together?

Say: "Then nobody moves in before Wednesday. I want the integrated test report signed before the first lease starts. Property manager, please hold move-ins until then."

Never say: "The fire marshal will check it anyway." Approval by an authority is not a substitute for your own proof that the systems work together. Professional sign-off required: fire protection engineer and commissioning authority, on integrated life-safety testing.

Scene four: the operator's question

The property manager asks: "When do I get the operations and maintenance manuals, the warranties and the as-built drawings? I cannot run the building without them."

The question behind the question: will the building's records arrive, or will the operator spend a year discovering it?

Say: "The closeout package is a condition of final payment, not a courtesy. Contractor, please give us the schedule for manuals, warranties, as-builts and spare parts by Friday, and we will hold final payment until it is complete and checked."

A second worked number, hypothetical. If the building's stabilised NOI is 1,920,000 dollars and each month of delayed lease-up costs about one twelfth of it, around 160,000 dollars of NOI, then holding move-ins a week to finish the integrated test costs about 37,000 dollars of NOI. That is small against the cost of occupying a building whose smoke control has not been proven. Say the number calmly; it makes the decision look like what it is, a priced choice.

Scene five: the lender's monitor

The lender's monitor asks: "What is the cost to complete, including the punch list, the closeout and the interest until the permanent loan funds? Is the loan still in balance?"

The question behind the question: is there a gap between finishing the building and the take-out that nobody has funded?

Say: "Cost to complete is the priced punch list, the remaining soft costs and interest for the months until the permanent loan funds. I will send you the reconciled figure, line by line against the undisbursed loan and remaining equity, by Thursday. If it shows a shortfall, the deposit will come with it."

Never say: "We are basically done, the numbers are fine." The months between substantial completion and stabilisation still carry interest, leasing costs and incentives, and an out-of-balance loan at this stage delays the very occupancy everyone wants.

Then add the one fact the monitor's lender most needs: the date you expect to meet the permanent lender's conditions, occupancy approval, a minimum level of leasing and an estoppel or rent-roll certificate, and what you will do if leasing runs slower than plan. If you do not know the leasing pace yet, say so and give the date you will.

Closing the meeting

Read back: "Merged punch list priced by Thursday. Holdback at one and a half times. Integrated life-safety report signed before move-in. Closeout schedule by Friday. Substantial completion certificate when the occupancy approval, the commissioning report and the priced list are in hand." Then ask the hardest question yourself: "Is there anything any of you knows that is not on the list?" Count to five in the silence.

Holding your state

Turnover meetings carry a particular fatigue: the end is in sight, and everyone wants it over. That is when concessions are made cheaply. Keep your pace slow, take the time you need to read each document before signing, and remember that the building will live for decades on the records you accept today.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is signing substantial completion and releasing retainage before the life-safety systems are proven together and the punch list is priced. The control is a written definition of done, agreed in the meeting, with each release tied to evidence.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner sees the contractor's relief and the operator's urgency and signs to keep goodwill. Goodwill survives a week's delay. It rarely survives a fire alarm that does not talk to the smoke control.

Callback

In Week 119, Idris taught commissioning, substantial versus final completion, occupancy certificates, punch lists and warranties. This scene is that lesson under pressure. In Week 117, Quincy and LEX taught retainage and holdbacks; the holdback calculation here is the same arithmetic used as leverage.

Recap

Define done in writing. Merge and price the punch list and hold back a multiple of it. Prove life-safety systems together before anyone moves in. Make the closeout package a condition of final payment. Read back, ask the hard question, wait.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: six questions, a Red Pen drill on the case's pro forma and the boardroom drill.
checklist: I agree in writing what substantial completion means before signing it.
I merge the contractor's and monitor's punch lists and price every item.
I hold back a multiple of open-item value from any retainage release.
No one moves in before integrated life-safety testing is signed.
The closeout package is a condition of final payment.
I can price a week of delayed lease-up in NOI.
I read back actions and ask whether anything is missing from the list.
head: Field checklist
speak: At substantial completion, everyone in the room wants the building called done: the contractor wants retainage, the operator wants to lease, the lender wants occupancy. I decide what done means, in writing. I sign substantial completion only with the occupancy approval, the commissioning authority's report and a priced punch list in hand. I merge the contractor's list with the monitor's, price every open item, and hold back about one and a half times that value from any retainage release, as the contract allows. Nobody moves in until the integrated fire alarm, smoke control and generator tests are signed. The manuals, warranties and as-built drawings are a condition of final payment. I can price the delay: a week of lost lease-up is about 37,000 dollars of NOI, small against occupying a building whose life-safety systems are unproven. Then I read back every action and ask if anything is missing.
terms: Substantial completion — the stage at which the building can be used for its purpose, though minor work remains, which often starts warranty and other contract periods.
Commissioning authority — an independent party who verifies that building systems are installed and work together as designed.
Closeout package — the manuals, warranties, as-built drawings, spare parts and certificates handed to the owner at the end of construction.

hostile.q: We are substantially complete under any reasonable reading. Why are you holding 1,400,000 dollars of retainage?
hostile.a: I am not holding it without reason, and I will show you the numbers. Under the contract, retainage moves at substantial completion against a priced punch list. The merged list prices open items at 200,000 dollars, so I am holding 300,000 dollars against that, and releasing the rest of the half you asked for, 800,000 dollars, as soon as the occupancy approval and the integrated life-safety report are signed. The remaining retainage follows the closeout package, as the contract says.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 130 Review: The Integrated Case
summary: Six questions test the integrated case: the master numbers, Stuyvesant Town and Rule 130, the take-out test, the chain of documents, the residual land value and the turnover meeting. A Red Pen drill on the case's pro forma summary and a two-minute boardroom drill close the week.
body:
The week came down to one sentence: one point of spread carries the whole building, and every gate, every loan and every document either protects that point or quietly spends it.

Recall

Q. In the case, what is the maximum permanent loan at 6 percent and 1.25 times coverage?

A. About 21,350,000 dollars: 1,920,000 dollars of NOI divided by 1.25 gives 1,536,000 dollars of debt service, at about 7.19 cents per dollar borrowed a year.

Q. What is a growing company's board for?

A. To oversee management, approve major decisions and test the numbers, so that the company is not run on one person's judgment alone.

Q. What makes an owner's meeting cadence effective on a construction project?

A. A fixed rhythm, a written agenda, decisions recorded with owners and dates, and escalation of anything unresolved before it becomes a dispute.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is the last ordinary review of the course. If you can answer these six questions aloud without notes, you can follow a building through its whole life and see how the parts connect. Answer each before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. State the case's master numbers and its development spread.

Answer: Total cost 32,000,000 dollars, stabilised NOI 1,920,000 dollars, yield on cost 6.0 percent, cap rate 5.0 percent, value 38,400,000 dollars, a one-point spread and a 20 percent profit on cost.

Question 2. What was the root cause at Stuyvesant Town, and what is Rule 130?

Answer: One assumption, rising income not yet allowed by law, tenants or market, passed through the price, the debt and the reserves without an independent test. Rule 130: at every gate, re-test the master assumption against evidence available today, and never let a price, loan or reserve depend on income not yet allowed.

Question 3. What happens to the take-out if the permanent rate rises from 6 to 7 percent?

Answer: The maximum loan falls to about 19,240,000 dollars, about 1,560,000 dollars short of the 20,800,000 dollar construction loan, with nothing wrong on site.

Question 4. Where do legal failures usually happen in the chain of documents?

Answer: Where two documents meet and do not fit: approval limits that differ between the contract, the joint venture agreement and the loan; a lease clause that law overrides; a will that conflicts with a partner's buy-out right.

Question 5. What is the residual land value at a 5.0 percent and a 5.5 percent cap rate?

Answer: 3,000,000 dollars at 5.0 percent and about 91,000 dollars at 5.5 percent, because land is a residual and absorbs every change in value.

Question 6. What must be true before anyone moves into the finished building?

Answer: The occupancy approval is issued and the integrated life-safety tests, fire alarm, smoke control and generator transfer, are signed.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Remi set out the case and its seven gates. Ford and Roman read Stuyvesant Town as a lifecycle failure and produced Rule 130. Priya ran the construction and permanent loans and the take-out test. LEX walked the chain of documents. Sage reverse engineered the land price and its fragility. Marco ran the turnover meeting.

The Red Pen

Read this hypothetical pro forma summary for the case and find the defects before reading on.

Pro forma summary, Gate 3. Gross potential rent 2,880,000. Other income 64,000. Operating costs 880,000. NOI 2,064,000. Total cost 32,000,000, of which contingency 1,000,000 is shown as a source of funds. Value at 5.0 percent: 41,280,000. Construction loan at 65 percent of value: 26,832,000. DSCR 1.25 on interest-only payments at 6 percent. Permanent loan: assumed equal to construction loan. Exit cap rate: 4.75 percent.

The defects. First, NOI omits vacancy and bad debt: 2,880,000 plus 64,000 less 880,000 is 2,064,000, but with 5 percent vacancy NOI is 1,920,000, so income is overstated by 144,000 dollars. Second, the inflated NOI flows into value, 41,280,000 instead of 38,400,000. Third, contingency is a cost, not a source of funds. Fourth, the construction loan is sized at 65 percent of value instead of cost; 65 percent of cost is 20,800,000 dollars, and sizing on an inflated value overstates it by about 6,000,000 dollars. Fifth, coverage is tested on interest-only payments, which ignores amortisation and flatters the permanent loan. Sixth, the permanent loan is assumed to equal the construction loan with no take-out test, which is exactly the gap Priya measured. Seventh, the exit cap rate of 4.75 percent is lower than the 5.0 percent used for value, with no reason given. Every defect moves in the same direction: toward a bigger, safer-looking deal.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes to a new partner who asks: "Walk me through this building from land to legacy." Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "It is a 100-unit building costing 32,000,000 dollars that earns 1,920,000 dollars of net operating income: a 6 percent yield on cost against a 5 percent market cap rate. That one point of spread is the reason to build, and the whole plan protects it. We paid 3,000,000 dollars for land, which is the residual at a 5 percent cap rate; at 5.5 percent it would support almost nothing, so we bought with conditions. The rent assumption is re-tested at every gate against today's evidence, which is Rule 130. We borrow 65 percent of cost to build and refinance on income; at 6 percent the permanent loan repays the construction loan, and at 7 percent it is about 1,560,000 dollars short, so that equity is committed in advance. The documents are mapped and checked where they meet. We do not occupy until the life-safety systems are proven together. And the shares are held in a structure our estate plan already accounts for."

Score yourself: bottom line first, the spread, one stress case, Rule 130, the take-out test, inside two minutes. If not, record again tomorrow.

Where to go back

If Question 1 or 5 was slow, rework Day 1 and Day 5 by hand: NOI from rent, vacancy, other income and costs; value at the cap rate; maximum cost at 1.20; land as the residual. If Question 2 was vague, reread Day 2 and say Rule 130 aloud until you can say it without notes, then name the master assumption of a building you know. If Question 3 was wrong, recompute the permanent loan at 6 and 7 percent: debt service of 1,536,000 dollars divided by about 0.0719 and about 0.0798. If Question 4 was thin, draw your own one-page document map for the case. If Question 6 was uncertain, reread Day 6 and Week 119 together.

A quick self-test, hypothetical. If the case's average rent were 2,300 dollars rather than 2,400 dollars, what happens to NOI? Gross potential rent falls by 120,000 dollars; after 5 percent vacancy, income falls by 114,000 dollars, so NOI is about 1,806,000 dollars. Yield on cost is about 5.64 percent, and the spread falls from one point to about 0.64. Work it aloud before checking.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is reading the parts of a building separately. The control is the one master table, re-run at every gate.

The beginner's mistake

Checking a pro forma's arithmetic and not its definitions. The Red Pen's numbers added up. Its definitions were wrong.

Callback

In Week 13, Sage taught sources and uses, contingency and estimate classes. The Red Pen's third defect, contingency as a source, was the first mistake that lesson warned against, and it is still the most common one in a pro forma, 117 weeks later.

Recap

One building, one point of spread, seven gates. Rule 130 re-tests the master assumption at each. Two loans, one take-out test. A chain of documents read at the joints. A residual land price that is fragile by nature. A turnover meeting that defines done in writing.

head: The six questions
speak: Our hypothetical building has 100 units, costs 32,000,000 dollars and earns 1,920,000 dollars of net operating income: a 6 percent yield on cost against a 5 percent cap rate, one point of spread that carries the whole plan. Land at 3,000,000 dollars is the residual at 5 percent; at 5.5 percent it would support almost nothing. Rule 130 says re-test the master assumption, the rent, at every gate against today's evidence. The construction loan is 65 percent of cost, 20,800,000 dollars. At 6 percent the permanent loan of about 21,350,000 dollars repays it; at 7 percent it falls about 1,560,000 dollars short, so I commit that equity in advance. The documents are mapped and checked where they meet. Nobody moves in until the life-safety systems are proven together. And in any pro forma, I check the definitions as well as the arithmetic: vacancy, contingency, the loan basis and the exit cap rate.
terms: Interest-only payment — a loan payment covering interest but no principal, which makes coverage look stronger than an amortising payment would.
Exit cap rate — the cap rate assumed when valuing the building at a future sale or refinance.
Gate — a go or no-go decision point with a named owner and a written decision.

hostile.q: Your summary shows 41,000,000 dollars of value and a 26,800,000 dollar construction loan. Your own lesson says 38,400,000 and 20,800,000. Which is true?
hostile.a: The lower numbers are true, and I withdraw the summary. It omitted 5 percent vacancy, which inflated NOI and value, and it sized the loan on value instead of cost. It also tested coverage on interest only and assumed the permanent loan would match the construction loan. The corrected version uses 1,920,000 dollars of NOI, a 20,800,000 dollar loan at 65 percent of cost, an amortising coverage test and a take-out test at 6 and 7 percent. I will send it today.
